Last year, Brian Rainez ran for U.S. Senate in North Dakota worried that the passage of a new controversial midschool bill would become the least discriminatory version of American policy in American history.

The Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA), which prohibits discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) Americans, was signed into law in 1990. It prohibits discrimination against anyone by their gender identity in active religious schools, at least on the basis of age and historical gender, and from employment discrimination based on race, religion, or disability. Ad Policy

The midschool bill marked a bold move toward marriage equality, becoming known as the Defense of Marriage Act of 1961 (CDISA). In particular, the midschool bill served as a section that is designed to protect lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender persons from discrimination based on race, gender, sexual orientation, or disability. Unlike any Act that has been decriminalized, the Education Against Americans Act was set up to make it illegal for teachers to discriminate based on religious beliefs under Section 1001 of the Defense of Marriage Act of 1952.
